#174560. Breaking: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

Breaking: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
  • Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m.
  • NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft debuted almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft debuted almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

According to recent reports, A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 released, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It has been revealed that it flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

Recent findings suggest that that's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that but you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

Sources indicate that the spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gustavo Varla is now up to 11 goals from his first 11 appearances in Serie A after netting a brace in Monza’s 3-0 victory over Fiorentina on Monday evening, which has seen the Biancorossi leapfrog their opponents in the Serie A table.

Goals from Varela (x2) and Jay Robinson handed Monza a much-needed three points in their Serie A match at home against Fiorentina on Sunday night, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone and into 14th place.

Fiorentina had begun the evening in 14th, but have dropped down to 16th as a result of tonight’s game, just one point above the drop zone after 12 matches.

Click here to see how today’s teams lined up.

Fiorentina were presented with the first real goalscoring opportunity after six minutes: Monza goalkeeper Demba Thiam, starting ahead of Noel Tornqvist, was off his line and managed to pass the ball straight to Christ Inaou Oulai under little pressure. Thiam was able to recover and make the save after the Ivorian’s weak shot at an empty net.

It was Monza who took the lead right at the end of the first half, though: Varela earning and converting a penalty kick just before stoppage time.

It has been revealed that the Portugal international had lined up a shot in a congested Fiorentina penalty area, which came off the arm of a flailing Oulai. The in-form Varela stepped up and converted into the right-hand side of the net, sending David De Gea the wrong way in the process.

As per Opta, Varela is one of only three players over the last 50 years to hit double digits for goals within their first 11 Serie A matches, along with Vincenzo Montella in 1997 and Diego Milito in 2008.

Recent findings suggest that varela’s second goal of the game came shortly after the re-start of the second half. Jay Robinson did well to shrug off Alex Jimenez before sending Matteo Pessina on the run down the left flank. Varela burst into the area and applied a smart, back-heel finish to convert Pessina’s low ball into the six-yard box for 2-0.

Robinson made it three less than 10 minutes later. Samuele Birindelli’s cross into the area was headed half-clear, but only as far as the Englishman on the edge of the area, who slammed a volley into the roof of the net with the help of a deflection on its way in.

Monza now find themselves in 14th place in the Serie A table, whilst Fiorentina have dropped down to 16th, one point above the relegation spots.

France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency

💡 Key Takeaways

  • UEFA, European football's governing body, stated it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, stated it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also confirmed his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

It has been revealed that he was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed.".

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

In a recent development, he has been facing growing criticism since pitching a initiative of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the strategy but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who remarked Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war.".

The German defense minister stated "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing.".

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts.".

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel.".

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over problems tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she rapidly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk noted he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges.".

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights.".

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl mentioned on Tuesday that the aims would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

In a recent development, france was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

In a recent development, the Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC mentioned that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, noted it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 newly introduced cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC mentioned it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also remarked arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

It has been revealed that the ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, noted the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, declared prepares to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl remarked on Tuesday that the looks would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp remarked that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

According to recent reports, "Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he mentioned.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the prepares, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These prepares allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement remarked.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's prepares are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he stated.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius confirmed on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the fresh funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He mentioned Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as fresh radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also noted that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and newly introduced transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the Upcoming York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also stated that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the initiative, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law.".

Meanwhile, more upcoming businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

Reports in Italy claim that Como have joined a list of Serie A sides interested in Manchester United and former Bologna attacker Joshua Zirkzee following a long-term set-back for Italy international Moise Kean in his recovery from injury.

Cesc Fabregas confirmed over the weekend that Kean is set to be sidelined for another few months, ‘not weeks’, following a set-back in training towards the end of last week.

Kean has been struggling with a recurring tibia problem for many months, a problem that has affected him for several months, before the completion of his €40m transfer to Como over the summer.

Since the summer, Kean has played through pain but has had set-backs along the way: His most recent appearance came for the Italy national team during the September-October international break.

Just as he was due to return to full training with Como, Kean suffered another setback, which may now require surgical intervention, and is expected to keep him out of action for another few months.

According to Monday’s reports from Gianluca Di Marzio, the setback suffered by Kean could lead Como to intervene in the January transfer window, and Manchester United’s Zirkzee could be a potential option.

The Netherlands international, who joined United from Bologna at an initial cost of €42.5m in the summer of 2024, is out of favour at Old Trafford and has not started in any of United’s competitive fixtures so far in 2026-27.

He has played for a total of 231 minutes across all competitions, divided across 11 substitute appearances in the Premier League, Champions League and EFL Cup.

Though he may have been considered surplus to requirements under former Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick, it remains to be seen how his predecessor, Mauricio Pochettino, will handle the Zirkzee situation.

Como are mentioned to be ‘exploring their options’, although there have not been any formal negotiations between them and Manchester United at this stage.

Como are not the only club interested in a potential deal for Zirkzee in January: Napoli will also be on the hunt for a new striker in the event that Lorenzo Lucca is moved on, and Gianluca Di Marzio claims that Zirkzee is of interest to them as well.

Zirkzee has previously been linked with moves to Juventus, Roma and Milan as well during his time at Old Trafford.

Lukaku, 33, unexpectedly announced his retirement from international football following Belgium's Nations League matches against Turkey and Italy earlier this month.

Belgium's all-time record goalscorer had been left on the bench against Italy, while he had not been in the squad three days earlier for the match against Turkey.

Lukaku's shock announcement caught Belgian media by surprise, while his former international team-mate Nainggolan has claimed more news will follow from the star.

Nainggolan, who won 30 caps for the national team between 2009 and 2018, revealed on the Ongefilterd Voetbal podcast he had a one-hour phone call with Lukaku following his decision.

Describing his international career as a 'great ride', Lukaku had confirmed his international retirement on social media.

'16 years old', his Instagram statement began. 'For 16 years, I gave everything for the national team. I experienced every possible emotion. I played with fantastic teammates for whom I will always be grateful.

Lukaku vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament.

Lukaku has captained Belgium on a handful of occasions since 2020, alongside the likes of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans.

Since Mark van Bommel's appointment in August, following Garcia's departure at the end of his contract, Lukaku has slipped further down the pecking order, with Charles De Ketelaere preferred to lead the line.

#174551. Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1179 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier remarked in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier remarked in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

Recent findings suggest that he also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the organization is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US manufacturer Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

According to recent reports, she says because the concern is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

In a recent development, "The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, states the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

Sources indicate that "If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she remarked. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

Industry observers note that it was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' blueprint to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

Industry observers note that "I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he noted. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".

It has been revealed that is artificial intelligence putting entry-level jobs in science at risk? As the technology increasingly takes on coding and basic data analysis, alongside other purely cognitive tasks, what will happen to graduate student and postdoctoral roles? And what does the future hold for programmers and technicians? These roles have conventionally been stepping stones to other scientific positions.

A 60-minute webinar organized by Nature’s Careers team will investigate how AI is transforming careers in science, as well as the technology’s short- and long-term impact on early-career researcher roles.

The live event takes place on 2 December at 15:00 GMT.

Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.
  • Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.
  • "Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp mentioned, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves.".

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

Sources indicate that it paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

In a recent development, the 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

It has been revealed that "I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp remarked after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired.".

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still noted it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong.".

Recent findings suggest that proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer.".

It has been revealed that while that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it.".

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In a recent development, in Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.

The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.

The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.

Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.

According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.

The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.

According to recent reports, the election of a newly introduced parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.

A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.

Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable tech giant in the space of a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable tech giant in the space of a month.

Recent findings suggest that since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the firm's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.".

Nvidia is calling the fresh group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones stated in a statement.

The tech giant did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was declared hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea.".

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Recent findings suggest that huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

That manufacturer, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

Manchester United have made signing a upcoming striker one of their main January priorities as Mauricio Pochettino looks for a more dependable option while Benjamin Šeško remains sidelined.

United have struggled badly this season and presently sit near the bottom of the Premier League, making immediate attacking reinforcement increasingly key.

Šeško is not expected back until January at the earliest, while Joshua Zirkzee has failed to provide consistent goals in his absence.

According to The Times, Man United will prioritise a centre-forward when the January window opens.

Pochettino wants greater reliability through the middle and United now have several weeks to assess potential targets.

Monaco striker Folarin Balogun is among the options being considered. The 25-year-old worked under Pochettino with the United States national team and could be available, with Monaco open to a departure.

United’s need has been increased by Šeško’s fitness problems, but there is no suggestion the club have given up on the Slovenia international.

A recent CaughtOffside report carried an update from Fabrizio Romano confirming there is “zero chance” of Šeško leaving in January, while United still intend to bring in another striker.

It has been revealed that šeško is only 23 and remains a major part of United’s long-term prepares. The problem is not necessarily his quality, but the lack of reliable cover when he is unavailable.

United therefore need a striker capable of contributing immediately without blocking Šeško once he returns.

Sources indicate that that makes someone like Balogun particularly interesting. He already knows Pochettino, has experience in English football and could offer mobility rather than simply duplicating Šeško’s physical profile.

Ivan Toney is another option who would provide proven Premier League quality, although his wages and the structure of any deal would need careful consideration.

The worst outcome would be another huge January fee for a striker signed out of panic.

United need goals now, but they also need a coherent plan.

The sensible solution is competition rather than replacement: add a striker who can immediately help Pochettino, while continuing to develop Šeško as the long-term No.9.

#174542. BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey

BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard.
  • After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury.
  • Industry observers note that on 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard.

After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–15 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.

Industry observers note that on 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.

It has been revealed that en route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, claims Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.

According to recent reports, for the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.

But beyond the money, Bellingham has been flourishing turning out for the Spanish giants – both on and off the pitch.

Here, Daily Mail Sport details Bellingham's lifestyle in Spain, and the rituals that have grounded the player after his explosion into superstardom.

Jude Bellingham is inching closer to a new deal at Real Madrid to become one of Europe's highest earners.

But more than just enjoying his football, Bellingham has made himself at home in the city (pictured at the Grand Prix of Spain in Madrid this year).

A recurring theme when Bellingham speaks of his love of living in Madrid stems from an established daily routine.

Speaking to his club just six months after he joined Los Blancos in the summer of 2023, Bellingham had already set up habits which helped him feel at home in the newly introduced city.

'I get up early to go to training, I train and then I head home,' Bellingham mentioned. 'Sometimes I'll go out for a coffee near home or head into town to grab something to eat. Then I go back home to chill out in the garden for a bit if the weather is good and the sun's out.

Industry observers note that 'If my friends are over, we'll go out for dinner and then back home. It's great. You get to know the people at the places you visit more often. Industry observers note that over two years later, and the patterns are no different. The Calvin Klein ambassador told Vogue this month that his ideal downtime involves 'being in the organization of my friends and family, having a coffee, going for a walk.

'You're always going to get recognised, but you're a bit safer in terms of not getting mobbed,' Bellingham stated of his favourite spots on the fringes of the city, where many of his repeat haunts are located.

Sources indicate that not that Bellingham is a little averse to integrating with the community. In fact, mingling with the locals has been a positive aspect of Bellingham's life abroad, with the player admitting in the summer of 2025 that Spain was very much 'home'.

Bellingham has connected with new head coach Jose Mourinho since his arrival in the summer.

'I can't cook, I can't drive… I'm good at what I do, but everything else?' he joked. 'Not that great.

In keeping with the idea that Bellingham has found his home in Spain, it stands to reason that the player has been working on his languages.

Confirming his aptitude for the language, Bellingham added: 'I think a big part of it is being confident enough to just speak.

'You know you're going to get stuff wrong, and you're probably not going to sound exactly right, (but if) people know what you're talking about, they'll probably think: "Fair play for trying".'.

American model Castro is a frequent fixture in the stands whether Bellingham is playing for Madrid or England.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup.".

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

It’s now been more than two years since Odysseas Vlachodimos made his one and only appearance for Newcastle United, but he remains on the books at St James’ Park.

The Greek goalkeeper was signed from Nottingham Forest by Eddie Howe in the summer of 2024 as part of the arrangement which saw Elliot Anderson going the other way, with his solitary outing coming against AFC Wimbledon during the triumphant Carabao Cup campaign.

The 32-year-old has been on loan at Sevilla since August of last year, having had the deal extended for another season, and he’s been a regular starter with the LaLiga outfit.

In an interview with El Desmarque, Vlachodimos was asked if he’d like to join the Andalusian club outright from Newcastle.

It has been revealed that he replied emphatically, and with a smile on his face: “I’ve already said it, yes. I really like the club and Spanish football. The club is like a family. I get along very well with all the players and coaches.

“I’m very happy here. My son also plays football here. He speaks Spanish better than I do, and the whole family is happy.”.

Having complained earlier this year about perceived broken promises at Newcastle, and with Lukas Hornicek joining over the summer, the likelihood of Vlachodimos ever playing for the Magpies again seems fanciful.

The Czech stopper is firmly the number one under Matthias Jaissle, with Nick Pope as his immediate deputy, and it’s hard to envisage the Greece international challenging that pecking order at St James’ Park.

He’ll be 34 by the time his contract expires in June 2028, and the Tyneside hierarchy might feel that next summer is the right time to cut the cord whilst the club can still bank a transfer fee for him.

Industry observers note that A permanent move to Sevilla would appear to be the ideal outcome for all parties. The LaLiga side would get to hold onto their first-choice goalkeeper, Vlachodimos can stay where he’s happy, and Newcastle would get his wages of approximately £50,000 per week off their books.

We’d expect that the two clubs will ultimately come to an agreement which’d see the goalkeeper become a Sevilla player outright and end his association with the Magpies.

Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The Latest York Times reports.
  • Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
  • Sources indicate that the year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The Latest York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

Sources indicate that the year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

It has been revealed that A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

Recent findings suggest that in Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

It has been revealed that "Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well.".

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily swiftly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

According to recent reports, in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

Sources indicate that so far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many early-career mathematicians are concerned about how AI models will affect their career prospects.Credit: Getty.

It has been revealed that AI company Anthropic has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most famous open problem in mathematics — with the help of its model Claude. The proposed proof, which is still being scrutinized, is the latest in a series of spectacular AI advances in mathematics that are upending the field.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

But the technology’s rapid progress is making early-career mathematicians anxious about the impact that it will have on their futures, according to two studies released in October.

One was a survey of graduate students and postdocs1 designed by three PhD students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge and uploaded to the preprint server arXiv. The other was conducted by the Martingale Foundation, a non-profit organization in London that supports postgraduate students. It surveyed people at all career stages, but the respondents were limited to UK mathematicians.

Key concerns included job security and feelings of demotivation — 70% of respondents to the student-led survey remarked that they were now more likely to consider careers outside academia.

Many mathematicians interviewed by Nature say that the survey results match what they have been hearing from their peers. Graduate students, in particular, feel that they need to develop their own skills and prove their worth at solving mathematical problems without AI. Some are also concerned about the long-term availability of academic jobs — and whether hard-won results produced by their human reasoning could be put them at a disadvantage in a job market where others use AI.

Source: Martindale Foundation report Mathematics in the Age of AI: The Impact on Postgraduate Experience.

It has been revealed that “The younger generation seems much more sceptical,” states Tasmin Chu, a mathematics PhD student at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. “Fundamentally, that’s because they are in a much worse material position.”.

The student-led survey found that only around 7% of the 268 voluntary respondents — most of whom were at US institutions — felt that AI developments would make it easier for them to get a job that would lead to an eventual professorship. Meanwhile, more than 75% of people expected it to become harder.

It has been revealed that only 13% of respondents said that they were letting AI tools produce papers for them from start to finish, although a majority of people said that they were using the tools for literature searches or finding mistakes in their papers. Of those respondents who do use AI tools, more than half said that they dislike doing so, and only around 30% said that they enjoy using them. More than three-quarters of respondents said that they would be unhappy if an AI model were to solve a problem that they had worked on (see ‘Pride in discovery’).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
  • This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.
