Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment.
  • It has been revealed that since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply.
  • "We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

It has been revealed that since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now claims overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," noted Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven.".

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she noted.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin remarked.

The UN now indicates that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors noted.

Failure to cut emissions swiftly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today.".

Industry observers note that he points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in newly introduced renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels rapidly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy looks focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering newly introduced ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system.".

In a recent development, france is sticking to a previously confirmed deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition blueprint.".

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

Sources indicate that and it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

In a recent development, scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she stated. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess.".

#174369. Mauricio Pochettino leaves incomplete legacy as USMNT tenure nears finish

Mauricio Pochettino leaves incomplete legacy as USMNT tenure nears finish

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that he raised the standard of U.S.
  • Sources indicate that if his departure overshadows the performance on the pitch, leaving the USMNT without a chance to win the Concacaf Nations League final for a second consecutive tournament, that will undo a significant portion of the good that he has accomplished by bringing along younger members of the squad.
  • Industry observers note that date: Saturday, Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that he raised the standard of U.S. Soccer. It's the first thing that you hear from multiple people as Mauricio Pochettino prepares to oversee his final two games. The reality is more mixed. His 1.91 points per game are the third-best of any manager to oversee the United States men's national team for more than 10 games, behind Gregg Berhalter and Bruce Arena, but he's also the first permanent manager since Steve Sampson to not win a Concacaf title, with the USMNT falling short in both the Concacaf Nations League and the Concacaf Gold Cup. That mentioned, it's hard to say that he isn't leaving the USMNT in a better place than he found it, although some credit should be given to U.S. Soccer and former sporting director Matt Crocker for that. It's a conflicted legacy that Pochettino will leave, but it's also one that can't be fully realized until after he oversees his final two matches against Haiti.

Sources indicate that if his departure overshadows the performance on the pitch, leaving the USMNT without a chance to win the Concacaf Nations League final for a second consecutive tournament, that will undo a significant portion of the good that he has accomplished by bringing along younger members of the squad. But as he prepares to depart, the USMNT exited the World Cup in the round of 16, the same stage as in 2022, and questions remain about how they'll hold up against the world's top teams. With the 2028 Olympics coming up and a latest training facility that allows space for the youth and senior sides to train in the same place, alongside the improvement in U.S. youth development thanks to MLS Next and MLS Next Pro, the USMNT were going to be in a good place no matter who took over at this stage, which is also what makes it critical to look at what comes next.

Industry observers note that date: Saturday, Nov. 14 | Time: 4:30 p.m. ET Location: Nu Stadium -- Miami, Florida TV: TNT | Live stream: HBO Max Odds: Haiti +750; Draw +440; USMNT -350.

According to recent reports, "Our ambition is high, and we believe that this is one of the great coaching jobs in the world. We have an experienced group of players; we've got a dynamic young pool of players," U.S. Soccer CEO JT Batson stated. "Last night, Mauricio, staff, and most of the men's team watched our U-20s play here at the national training center, which was a pretty special moment. We publicly shared our ambition is to be in a position where we're winning major tournaments, including World Cups, and we want to make sure that we're attracting leaders who help us do just that. We know from our experience that great leaders want to work with great people, and great leaders want to make an impact on things that matter, and we think that we've proven at U.S. Soccer that we're a great place to work and we're a great place to make legacy-defining impact.".

Industry observers note that call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

U.S. Soccer is still in talks to hire a director of soccer who will work with the incoming head coach, United States women's national team coach Emma Hayes and the rest of the U.S. Soccer staff to shape the vision of American soccer. The sport is growing rapidly here, which is what makes this such an attractive job even without the shine of hosting a men's World Cup on home soil to add to the sales pitch. Listening to Batson, while BJ Callaghan may be one of the top American fits for the role, you can easily see why the USMNT would like to bring in Pep Guardiola if they can, and there's a sales pitch there to at least get top targets to pick up the phone.

This doesn't diminish what Pochettino has done while leading the national team, but each manager has made his mark on American soccer in his own way. Jurgen Klinsmann added legitimacy to the USMNT role and ushered in an era of German Americans who led the squad to upcoming heights. Gregg Berhalter came in, raised the floor for the squad, did excellent work with dual-national recruitment and led the squad out of its group at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Sure, in hindsight, things should've ended there, with U.S. Soccer moving in a different direction after the World Cup, but the players also wanted continuity.

In a recent development, you can make the same argument that Pochettino maybe shouldn't have been signed to a new contract following the World Cup, but even he seemed to believe that an opportunity such as Manchester United wouldn't have come this quickly. If he were leaving in 2028, after Steve Cherundolo led the U.S. U-23s on a strong run in the Olympics, the departure wouldn't be as bittersweet as this one, which feels like a job left unfinished by the Argentine.

It has been revealed that pochettino did add confidence, and to hear players like Sebastian Berhalter, Cavan Sullivan, Alex Freeman and Neil Pierre, among others, tell it, when Pochettino was at his best, this team would press anyone off the pitch. Now the onus is on the players to take that forward under fresh management.

"I think Poch definitely raised the standard since he's been in charge. I think you guys have seen that, just the intensity of training, how we approach games, he's changed our way of thinking as players, from calling the friendlies that we have in certain camps official games, not official games. He wants us to just be of a mindset to go out there and win," Folarin Balogun stated.

Sources indicate that "He's laid the foundation, and I think we, as players, have that ownership to not just do that because Poch was in charge; I think we have the ownership as players to carry that out because we know the standard," he continued. "So yeah, I think that's the benefit of having a top coach, and I'm sure you know whether he's here or not, the US will look to replace him with another top coach.".

A tearful Pochettino and the disappointed players show that this didn't end the way anyone would've wanted, but that doesn't mean there isn't plenty of good to build on for whoever comes next. With Cherundolo leading the December camp, there's plenty of time to ensure that the next hire is the right one, but now that U.S. Soccer has shown that it can recruit a coach of Pochettino's caliber, there's no reason to stop there. Having a coach coveted by others is a product of success, but having a system that can move past that proves things are sustainable.

The word "sustainable" hasn't been one that U.S. Soccer has been able to use as of late, as one thing going wrong could lead to a spiral, but with benefactors, facilities and youth all at once, it's time to build a future that isn't dependent on who the coach is, because that's what will lead to winning a World Cup.

#174367. Build for the future climate — or waste trillions of dollars

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1848 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Build for the future climate — or waste trillions of dollars

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, reservoirs need to be constructed in ways that help to avoid water shortages as heatwaves increase.
  • According to recent reports, “Prepare for El Niño”, the World Meteorological Organization warned earlier this year.
  • It has been revealed that repeated disasters cause immense disruption to people’s lives and livelihoods, and the economic loss and damage can add up to trillions of dollars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, reservoirs need to be constructed in ways that help to avoid water shortages as heatwaves increase. Credit: Ander Gillenea/AFP via Getty.

According to recent reports, “Prepare for El Niño”, the World Meteorological Organization warned earlier this year. Governments are responding by adjusting agricultural practices and securing water supplies. But climate measures should not begin when a hazardous event approaches, they should be part of a wider strategy of planning for a warmer future.

It has been revealed that repeated disasters cause immense disruption to people’s lives and livelihoods, and the economic loss and damage can add up to trillions of dollars. Climate warnings and actions taken in anticipation of disasters can help to reduce the impact on people and economies. But their effectiveness is constrained by existing limitations, such as a community’s access to resources and infrastructure.

Such vulnerabilities must be addressed at their source, when decisions about development and infrastructure are being made, so that climate risks are reduced through better planning rather than through reactive responses to individual events. Decisions about the location and capacity of reservoirs, agricultural drainage systems and the design of cities and transport infrastructure, for instance, cannot be changed easily once they have been made.

Much of what is being built now will shape societies for decades. To meet global climate and development objectives by 2030, nearly US$7 trillion of infrastructure investment is needed annually1. Global annual infrastructure spending is projected to increase from $4.4 trillion in 2024 to $6.9 trillion by 20502. But it will be wasted if projects are designed inadequately for the climate conditions that people will face.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too.

Decisions for development projects are being hampered because climate projections are often not integrated into planning processes. Another challenge is the limited availability of reliable, decision-relevant climate information for the 5–30-year period — an intermediate timescale between seasonal forecasts and long-term climate projections that is particularly relevant for planning major infrastructure such as roads and reservoirs3.

It has been revealed that climate services can provide this information. Scientists can improve climate projections. Development planners can assess projects. But unless these functions are connected within the development process, the system as a whole remains reactive.

Industry observers note that A common operating system would change that. Government ministries that oversee development would determine which planning decisions need to consider climate information. Planning institutions would ensure that climate assessments are undertaken and considered as part of investment approval for climate-sensitive projects. Climate agencies would provide the scientific information, which would improve both planning and science. Here, I outline how such a system would work.

A central government planning institution should establish a small climate-planning unit within it, not separately. Corresponding units could be set up in state or subnational planning institutions when appropriate. In countries without central planning institutions, the same functions could be assigned to existing government institutions.

The central unit would set common standards, consolidate information needs across sectors and jurisdictions, coordinate with national climate agencies and ensure that climate considerations are incorporated into the planning and appraisal of projects of national significance. Subnational units would apply the framework to local projects and feed emerging requirements back to the central unit.

Industry observers note that responsibilities should be made explicit. Ministries should identify the climate information needed to support various sectors. Planning institutions would coordinate those needs and ensure that such climate information informs investment decisions. Climate agencies would produce the underlying scientific information and ensure its technical accuracy and quality.

According to recent reports, this division matters. The proposal is not to make development planners become climate scientists, nor to make climate agencies become development authorities. It is to give them a permanent institutional connection.

The rules governing public investment in development should be changed to follow this principle: funding for a major climate-sensitive project should not be approved without a demonstration that it has been designed for the climate it is expected to face.

In a recent development, governments should request climate assessments for large, long-lived and climate-sensitive projects before approving funds. Assessments should be provided early enough in the process to influence the location, technology, scale and design of a project. For a upcoming reservoir, for example, the relevant planning unit would identify the climate conditions that the reservoir is likely to face during its operational lifetime, with implications for where and how it is built.

It has been revealed that A climate-planning unit would not decide whether the project should proceed; it would certify that the relevant climate risks have been assessed and that reasonable alternatives have been considered. Its assessment would be considered as part of an investment appraisal alongside economic, technical, social and environmental factors.

To be effective, the system must connect three functions: development demand, climate analysis and investment approval.

According to recent reports, ministries should periodically identify the climate information needed for their forthcoming development decisions. The central planning unit should consolidate these requests and work with climate agencies to determine what information can be provided, what projects require fresh analysis and when investment for climate observations, modelling or scientific capacity is needed.

Kenya’s government is implementing measures to reduce flooding from rivers.Credit: James Wakibia/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty.

This comprehensive approach would provide climate scientists with clear directives from the development system. It would encourage them to improve climate projections for specific regions, over a 5–30-year typical planning horizon, and for distinct sectors. It would also reduce the need for individual development projects to commission their own climate analyses, which can be patchy and inconsistent.

In a recent development, an analysis of six generations of assessment reports from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found, for instance, that inconsistent climate projections across many low- and middle-income countries were complicating adaptation and long-term planning efforts4. For example, in some regions, precipitation was projected by one assessment to increase, and by the next to decrease, with successive views bouncing back and forth.

Such disagreements undermine a region’s ability to make long-term investments. They increase the likelihood of costly misallocation of funds, maladaptation to climate risks and infrastructure being developed that is ill-suited to future climate conditions. Dams, cities and transport corridors cannot be easily redesigned or rebuilt once constructed.

This challenge is compounded by the fact that climate models perform poorly across many climate-vulnerable regions. In South Asia, for example, simulations of temperature and precipitation can differ from observed values by as much as 25% and 100%, respectively5. Such biases limit the reliability of model-based climate information for guiding long-term development decisions.

It has been revealed that that’s why the proposed climate-informed planning units would ensure that climate agencies’ work is guided by clearly articulated development needs and that the information they provide is reliable and fit for development planning. Importantly, they would not be a replacement for other climate services, which can remain focused on providing accurate information for a wide range of sectors6,7. The aim is to bridge a specific gap between climate information and development.

A climate assessment for a development project should not become obsolete as soon as the work is approved. Both central and subnational planning units should regularly monitor whether new climate observations or scientific assessments change the climate risks identified. If they do, an updated assessment should be returned to the planning authority.

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming.

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming.

In a recent development, the units should evaluate whether the climate information generated by the system is useful. Regular technical reviews would compare climate projections with observations and assess whether the information remains fit for planning purposes. Institutional reviews conducted by climate-planning units could also examine whether big projects have incorporated climate foresight and whether it influenced their designs.

It has been revealed that these reviews would create a feedback loop. Development decisions would determine what information is needed, which could be satisfied by climate-science and investment-appraisal processes. Data from implemented projects would then be fed back into the system to upgrade climate information and plans going forwards.

Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (329 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa intends to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a organization letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
  • The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa intends to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a organization letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

Recent findings suggest that this is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that the executive board mentioned on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful.".

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter stated.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

The firm also aims to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Sources indicate that furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.
